methodology: Authorized runtime route and schema verification. HTTP method existence was primarily proven with unauthenticated GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH requests that stop at Lucky authentication; method discovery does not execute protected mutating handlers. Selected GET routes were additionally verified with the repository OpenToken client. Request schemas were recovered from frontend pass-through/object literals and, where applicable, cross-checked against authorized read-only GET shapes. For nested-schema enrichment, current Lucky 3.0.0 frontend bundles were inspected only in memory and authorized GET responses were reduced to field names/JSON types; live domains, identifiers, paths, addresses and secret values were not persisted. Where frontend/read-only evidence was insufficient and the instance owner explicitly authorized it, selected routes used bounded API write probes against newly created disposable resources, followed by immediate cleanup and baseline verification; each such route records its exact boundary in schema_evidence. Dangerous/global operations were not exercised against existing business resources. For the six Docker legacy wrappers that lacked current UI call sites, upgrade/build used dedicated disposable BusyBox resources, Git/ZIP/import used validation-failure paths, and prune was exercised only by a temporary Lucky instance connected to a non-destructive mock Docker API. No real Docker prune handler reached the production Docker daemon.

same_bundle_prefix_artifacts.description: Literal-only paths that are strict prefixes of method-bearing routes from the same frontend bundle. Runtime probing confirmed no additional standalone method beyond already cataloged generic/template matches; PATCH probes were also 404. Suppression is version-bound and is not performed by the generic extractor.

ipdb_behavior.verification: A bounded Lucky 3.0.0 probe started from an empty IPDB item baseline, downloaded a public GeoCN MMDB into memory, uploaded two uniquely named TEST copies through Lucky, created a disabled geocn item, PUT-updated its buffer mode, enabled it through the GET boolean route, and waited for Ready=true. The item was then switched to the second uploaded TEST file and lookup succeeded again. The item and both DB files were removed and the original item Key baseline was restored.

ddns_cloudflare_behavior.verification: On an authorized Lucky 3.0.0 instance, a bounded probe cloned only the in-memory Cloudflare provider configuration of an existing task, created a unique TEST Cloudflare A record and a unique disabled TEST DDNS task, read it back, PUT-updated it, toggled disable/enable, and served an IPv4 result from a loopback HTTP endpoint. Enabling the task resolved {ipv4Addr} from that endpoint and updated the independent Cloudflare test record from one documentation-range address to another. The probe then PUT-changed only the disposable record value to a second documentation-range literal, invoked manualSync, and independently verified Cloudflare changed to that second value. A webhook test performed a real loopback POST and received the expected success content. Finally the TEST task and DNS record were deleted; the original TaskKey set was restored and no TEST task or Cloudflare record remained. Provider credentials, real business domains/addresses and webhook contents are intentionally not retained.

observations.create_validation: Lucky rejects an A-record task whose normalized SyncRecordData.ipv4Address is empty, even when the task is initially disabled
observations.template_semantics: The existing working Cloudflare task uses {ipv4Addr}; it is a substitution template rather than a cached literal IP
observations.manual_sync: A deterministic PUT of the TEST record's desired literal value followed by manualSync caused a real Cloudflare update; URL refresh behavior was proven separately by the enable-triggered query
observations.cleanup: Cloudflare test record absent, zero TEST DDNS tasks, and the original non-TEST TaskKey set restored

ddns_cloudflare_behavior.security: The probe never prints or persists DNS provider credentials. It creates only uniquely prefixed TEST tasks and Cloudflare records, uses documentation-range IPs plus loopback HTTP endpoints, and cleans both Lucky and Cloudflare resources in a finally path.

webservice_reverseproxy_semantics.frontend_evidence: Lucky 3.0.0's shared WebService rule/subrule editor exposes NginxConf as a mini-nginx configuration field and documents proxy_set_header, proxy_hide_header, add_header, proxy_redirect, location and Lucky's path shorthand. The editor also exposes UseTargetHost, AutoProxyLocation, AutoProxyLocationWithoutSameHost, AddProtoToHeader/ProtoHeaderKey and AddRemoteIPToHeader/AddRemoteIPHeaderKey. The current frontend saves subrule edits by reading the complete parent WebService rule, changing DefaultProxy/ProxyList, and PUTing the preserved parent object back to /api/webservice/rule/{RuleKey}; copied/new subrules use an empty/unset Key and receive a Key from Lucky after persistence.

model.write_model: GET complete parent rule -> preserve unrelated fields -> edit/append DefaultProxy or ProxyList -> PUT complete parent rule; a newly appended subrule has no existing Key and Lucky assigns one

NginxConf.syntax: semicolon-terminated directives; # comments and quoted values with spaces are accepted

model.UseTargetHost: boolean; true sends the target URL host as the upstream Host header, false preserves the frontend request host
model.AutoProxyLocation: boolean; when enabled Lucky rewrites qualifying upstream redirects through a frontend lucky_auto_reverseproxy_<opaque-token>/ path
model.AutoProxyLocationWithoutSameHost: boolean; with AutoProxyLocation enabled, true leaves same-upstream-host redirects unchanged and rewrites redirects to a different host
model.AddProtoToHeader: boolean paired with ProtoHeaderKey; writes the client-side scheme into the configured upstream request header
model.AddRemoteIPToHeader: boolean paired with AddRemoteIPHeaderKey; writes the client address into the configured upstream request header
model.path_matching: Domains may include a frontend path prefix. Lucky removes that frontend prefix before location/path matching, then joins the remaining request path to any path already present in Locations; query parameters are preserved. $request_uri, $uri and $document_uri were observed with the frontend path still present.

webservice_reverseproxy_semantics.verification: On an authorized Lucky 3.0.0 production listener, a bounded probe added ten uniquely named TEST reverse-proxy subrules in one parent-rule PUT, exercised them through the existing TLS listener against an external echo/redirect origin, then removed only those TEST subrules from the latest parent rule. Runtime checks verified literal and variable proxy_set_header values, empty-value request-header removal, proxy_hide_header, add_header default status behavior and always, proxy_redirect for Location and Refresh, location prefix/exact/regex/case-insensitive-regex/negative matching, path wildcard/regexp/negative matching, frontend-prefix stripping plus upstream-base-path joining, query preservation, UseTargetHost, protocol/client-IP helper headers, AutoProxyLocation modes, and proxy_redirect off/default compatibility. The final business subrule list was byte-for-byte equal at the JSON-object level and no TEST subrule remained. Live hostnames, rule identifiers, client addresses and generated redirect tokens are intentionally omitted.

observations.add_header: without always it was present on 200 and absent on 418; with always it was present on both
observations.proxy_redirect: an explicit From/To mapping rewrote both Location and Refresh; proxy_redirect off preserved the raw redirect; proxy_redirect default was accepted and left both unrelated and same-upstream-host redirects raw in this probe
observations.auto_proxy_location: enabled mode rewrote both same-host and different-host redirects to a frontend /<prefix>/lucky_auto_reverseproxy_<opaque-token>/... path; AutoProxyLocationWithoutSameHost=true preserved same-host redirects while still rewriting different-host redirects
observations.connection_upgrade: $connection_upgrade expanded to upgrade for a request carrying Upgrade: websocket and Connection: Upgrade in the final verification run

webservice_reverseproxy_semantics.security: NginxConf is powerful configuration, not a safe template language. Do not interpolate untrusted user strings into directives. Parent-rule PUT is a whole-object replacement: re-read immediately before a write, preserve unknown/unrelated fields, minimize writes, and clean disposable probes by removing only their unique TEST-prefixed subrules from the latest object instead of restoring a stale snapshot.

webservice_sni_routing.frontend_evidence: Lucky 3.0.0 frontend service-type options expose the exact value SNIRouting; the SNI editor labels Locations as the SNI routing target address and requires parent-rule TLS.

model.Locations: array of raw TCP target strings in host:port form

webservice_sni_routing.verification: On an authorized production instance, a preserved WebService rule was updated with one new SNIRouting subrule, re-read successfully, and external TLS traffic matched by SNI was forwarded bidirectionally to a local TLS service. The target service presented the hostname certificate and completed an authenticated HTTPS CONNECT tunnel plus a read-only Git smart-HTTP ls-remote request. Unauthenticated proxy access returned 407 and an authenticated CONNECT to a non-allowlisted target returned 403. Live domain names, rule identifiers, addresses, ports and credentials are intentionally omitted.
webservice_sni_routing.limits: Current Lucky 3.0.0 frontend reports a maximum of six SNI routing rules per WebService rule. SNI routing is TLS passthrough, so the target service must terminate TLS and present a certificate valid for the SNI hostname.

model.MappingChangeScript: string command executed after mapped certificate content changes

ssl_certificate_mapping.verification: On an authorized Lucky 3.0.0 certificate managed by ACME, a disposable TEST certificate was created with MappingToPath already enabled before issuance. Lucky wrote non-empty <Remark>.key, <Remark>.crt and <Remark>.pem files into a unique TEST directory; the files were observed through Lucky's own local-path-browser API because the production Lucky runs in Docker and its /tmp namespace is not the host /tmp. Earlier bounded runs also showed that switching MappingToPath from false to true after an already-issued certificate did not immediately backfill old certificate material; mapping is tied to certificate material creation/change rather than a pure config toggle. Separate prior mapping verification found the mapped private key initially mode 0644 and reduced it to 0600 with MappingChangeScript configured to re-apply the restrictive mode. Certificate bodies, private keys, DNS API credentials, ACME account data and filesystem paths are intentionally omitted.
ssl_certificate_mapping.security: GET /api/ssl/{param} can return CertBase64 and KeyBase64. Do not print or persist raw responses; use redaction or root-only temporary files, and remove temporary secret-bearing payloads immediately after a reviewed update.

model.issuance: A unique TEST DNS hostname using an in-memory clone of an existing ACME/DNS-provider configuration reached issued state with the requested hostname in certificate metadata and a SHA-256 fingerprint

model.manual_sync: GET /api/ssl/manualsync/{Key} reaches the certificate sync business path; whether transfer occurs depends on configured sync clients and instance entitlement

ssl_acme_behavior.verification: A bounded Lucky 3.0.0 probe created one unique TEST ACME certificate, waited for real issuance, verified hostname/fingerprint/validity metadata and certificate-material presence without persisting the material, verified MappingToPath files through Lucky's own filesystem browser, PUT-updated the disposable object, toggled it off/on, exercised manualsync and flush only on that TEST certificate, then deleted it and its TEST mapping directory. The original certificate Key set was restored and no TEST certificate remained.

observations.mapping_namespace: Lucky runs in Docker with its own /tmp namespace; mapping verification must use a Lucky-visible path/API or an explicitly shared mount rather than assuming host /tmp is the same filesystem
observations.mapping_lifecycle: Enabling mapping before issuance produced key/crt/pem files; enabling it only after existing material was already issued did not immediately backfill files in bounded runs
observations.flush: The valid TEST certificate remained issued and its fingerprint did not change after flush in the final run
observations.cleanup: The TEST certificate Key baseline was restored and the unique Lucky-side mapping directory was removed

ssl_acme_behavior.security: The probe clones existing ACME/DNS-provider fields only in memory, never prints certificate/private-key/provider material, mutates only a unique TEST certificate, and removes only its own TEST filesystem directory.

observations.cleanup: No TEST sync client or TEST certificate remained; temporary SSH authorization and target/key directories were removed

ssl_sync_client_behavior.security: The probe does not bypass Lucky entitlement. It uses a localhost-only disposable SSH credential, unique TEST sync client/certificate/paths, preserves current non-TEST SSL settings from the latest object, and never emits SSH or certificate private keys.

webterminal_behavior.verification: Two bounded probes exercised WebTerminal end to end. The local probe created a TEST local /bin/sh connection, opened a real ticketed WebSocket, sent resize and shell input, observed output, inspected/listed/remarked/statted the session, detached and re-attached it, then closed the session and removed the connection. The SSH/SFTP probe used the existing localhost sshd with one ephemeral key, exercised Lucky's first-use host-key trust flow and a real SSH terminal, then performed isolated SFTP file and tar.gz archive operations under /tmp. All TEST connection/session/authorization/path baselines were restored. Multipart and streaming upload failures were reproduced after matching the current frontend request shapes exactly.

observations.websocket_packetization: Lucky may send the first WebSocket frame in the same TCP read as the HTTP 101 response; the shared stdlib RFC6455 helper now preserves those post-header bytes instead of assuming packet boundaries are protocol boundaries
observations.host_key_confirmation: The first test returned ret=409 with host/port/hostname/hostKey/fingerprint/trustedAt/keyType fields; after persisting trust, a second test with the disposable private key returned ret=0
observations.multipart_upload_failure: POST /api/webterminal/sftp/{SessionId}/upload returned ret=5 SSH_FX_FAILURE even after FormData field order was matched to file -> path -> filename
observations.streaming_upload_failure: POST /api/webterminal/sftp/{SessionId}/upload-streaming returned closed-pipe semantics for a small body and ret=4 closed-pipe / BrokenPipe behavior for a 1 MiB body
observations.cleanup: No TEST WebTerminal connection/session, temporary SSH authorization, key directory or TEST file tree remained after the final probes

webterminal_behavior.security: WebTerminal probes are intentionally high-risk and therefore constrained to localhost, unique TEST resources and /tmp. The SSH key is ephemeral and forwarding/X11/agent use is disabled; terminal output, host-key material, private keys and file contents are not persisted in evidence.

model.litelist: GET /api/storagemanagement/litelist contains enabled items only in the verified local-storage flow: the TEST item disappeared after disable and reappeared after enable
model.system_mount: SystemMount remained disabled throughout this probe; no OS mount behavior is claimed

storagemanagement_local_behavior.verification: Starting from empty list and litelist baselines on an authorized Lucky 3.0.0 Linux instance, a bounded probe created one Lucky-visible /tmp/TEST-* directory through local-path-browser and POSTed one TEST local storage item. Runtime readback confirmed Type=local, the TEST LocalPath and disabled SystemMount, while also revealing that creation normalized Enable to true. The probe explicitly disabled the item, verified its absence from litelist, PUT-updated Remark and Writable while disabled, enabled it and verified litelist exposure, disabled it again, read module logs, deleted the storage item and TEST path, and confirmed both storage and litelist Key baselines were restored.

observations.create_forces_enable_true: The final probe sent Enable=false in the create body but the first persisted readback was Enable=true
observations.readback_shape: The full item readback exposed Enable, Info, Key, Log, MountMsg, Params, Remark, SystemMount, Type and Writable; local Params retained LocalPath and SystemMount remained disabled
observations.litelist_filter: The disabled TEST item was absent from litelist and the enabled TEST item appeared with Detail, Key, Remark and Writable fields
observations.cleanup: Zero TEST storage items remained, the Lucky-visible TEST path was removed, and both full-list and litelist Key baselines were restored

storagemanagement_local_behavior.security: The probe creates only a unique Lucky-visible /tmp directory and one TEST local storage item. It never enables SystemMount, never changes existing storage items, and deletes only its own TEST item/path. WebDAV behavior testing separately verifies consumer-side Writable enforcement; OS mounting remains unverified.

model.principal_model: A WebDAV user uses Username, Password, Prefix, FrontType, Modify and MountList; the verified mount model uses Type, Param, DisplayName and Writable
model.protocol: A loopback HTTP WebDAV listener answered OPTIONS with a DAV header and PROPFIND with a successful multi-status response exposing both TEST mounts

model.isolation: The verified service bound only 127.0.0.1 on a random high port with TLS disabled and AutoFirewall=false

webdav_storage_behavior.verification: With the existing WebDAV service stopped and Users empty, a bounded Lucky 3.0.0 probe created two unique local StorageManagement TEST items and paths, one writable and one read-only. It temporarily configured one disposable Basic-auth WebDAV user with store mounts named rw and ro, started WebDAV on 127.0.0.1, verified OPTIONS/PROPFIND, performed a real PUT/GET/DELETE against the writable mount, and verified PUT to the read-only mount was rejected with no file created. It read module logs, then restored the exact original WebDAV configuration only after re-checking that the live config still carried the probe's unique username/port ownership markers. WebDAV status/users, Storage keys and TEST paths all returned to baseline.

observations.writable_mount: PUT, GET and DELETE succeeded and the Lucky-visible backing path reflected create/remove operations
observations.readonly_mount: PUT returned HTTP 404 in the verified run and the backing path remained free of the attempted file
observations.readback: WebDAV user readback exposed Dir, FrontType, Modify, MountList, NoSniff, Password, Prefix and Username; mount readback exposed DisplayName, InvalidMsg, IsLocalDir, Param, Type and Writable
observations.cleanup: Original stopped WebDAV configuration and empty-user baseline were restored; two TEST storages and both TEST paths were removed

webdav_storage_behavior.security: The probe refuses to run when WebDAV is already active or has configured users, binds only loopback, disables firewall automation and TLS, uses a disposable random password, and never prints credentials or file content. Configuration restoration is ownership-guarded to avoid overwriting a concurrent change.

model.service_lifecycle: PUT /api/ftpserver/configure starts and stops the FTP service on Lucky 3.0.0; the successful CI probe started from the fresh stopped/empty baseline, applied one TEST configuration, then restored the exact baseline through the API
model.principal_model: A working FTP user accepts Username, Password and one local MountList. Runtime readback verified Username and Dirs as strings, ReadOnly as boolean and MountList as an array; credential values are never retained. The local mount readback verified Type, Param and DisplayName as strings plus Writable and IsLocalDir as booleans
model.protocol: A Python stdlib FTP client completed passive-mode login, directory listing, STOR upload, RETR download and DELE against the disposable Lucky service; a wrong password was rejected
model.root_mapping: With exactly one local mount, the mounted directory is the FTP root itself rather than an extra DisplayName subdirectory: a seed file placed directly in the mounted directory appeared in root LIST/NLST and an uploaded file appeared directly in the same backing directory
model.passive_range: Lucky 3.0.0 rejects a PassivePortStart/PassivePortEnd range whose difference is below 9; the final probe uses ten consecutive passive ports and disables active mode
model.isolation: The probe runs only under GitHub Actions with a fresh pinned Lucky 3.0.0 container. Admin, FTP control and all passive ports are Docker-published only on runner 127.0.0.1, AutoFireWall is disabled, TLS is not required and no RS production listener or firewall is changed

ftp_ci_behavior.verification: A GitHub-hosted CI run of tools/lucky_ftp_ci_probe.py used the pinned Lucky 3.0.0 image and configured the disposable instance exclusively through Lucky HTTP APIs after OpenToken bootstrap. The probe verified the fresh FTP baseline was stopped with no users, started one TEST account and local mount, confirmed all published admin/control/passive ports were runner-loopback-only, rejected a wrong password, completed real passive FTP login/list/upload/download/delete with byte-for-byte backing-file checks, read status plus both log surfaces, then PUT-restored the original stopped configuration and removed the container. The final successful run reported failed=[] and Lucky version 3.0.0.

observations.authentication: The disposable TEST account accepted the generated password and rejected the same username with an incorrect password
observations.list_and_transfer: Root directory listing saw the pre-created seed file; STOR created the exact marker bytes in the mounted backing directory, RETR returned the same bytes and DELE removed the backing file
observations.readback: Safe FTP user readback types were Dirs=string, MountList=array, ReadOnly=boolean and Username=string. Safe mount types were DisplayName/Param/Type=string and IsLocalDir/Writable=boolean; the live Password value and all generated credentials were omitted from evidence
observations.cleanup: The exact fresh stopped FTP configuration was restored through the API after an ownership check, and the disposable Lucky container plus TEST directory were removed by runner teardown

ftp_ci_behavior.security: The FTP probe is CI-only and refuses local execution. Because Lucky FTP has no ListenIP field, isolation is enforced outside Lucky by publishing every FTP port only to runner loopback; active mode and AutoFireWall are disabled. No production Lucky configuration, host firewall, public listener, password value or transferred marker content is retained.

model.device_lifecycle: A disposable WOL device can be created and deleted through /api/wol/device while preserving an empty device baseline; BroadcastIPs accepts string broadcast-address entries
model.service_lifecycle: On a fresh Lucky 3.0.0 instance the WOL Server and Client are disabled. The CI probe temporarily enables only Server.Enable through /api/wol/service/configure, verifies the enabled readback, then restores both disabled states
model.wake_packet: GET /api/wol/device/wakeup?key=<owned TEST key> returned ret=0 and emitted the exact standard 102-byte magic packet: six 0xff bytes followed by sixteen repetitions of the six-byte TEST MAC
model.destination_port: The captured wake datagram used UDP destination port 9 even though the disposable device was configured with a different random Port value; current Lucky 3.0.0 wakeup behavior therefore does not use that device Port field for the emitted magic packet
model.state_boundary: The disposable device reported CanWakeup=true while State was Unknown and no real powered endpoint existed. This verifies packet emission, not an actual machine transition from offline to online; shutdown remains intentionally unexercised
model.isolation: The probe runs only in GitHub Actions with a fresh pinned Lucky 3.0.0 container attached to a Docker --internal bridge. The admin port is not published, the wake destination is only that bridge's private broadcast address, and raw capture is bound only to the uniquely named internal bridge

wol_ci_behavior.verification: A GitHub-hosted CI run of tools/lucky_wol_ci_probe.py created a disposable Docker --internal bridge and a pinned Lucky 3.0.0 container whose admin port was not published. After API login/OpenToken bootstrap, the probe confirmed an empty WOL device baseline and disabled Server/Client baseline, temporarily enabled only the WOL Server, then created one TEST device with a locally administered random MAC and the internal bridge broadcast address. The device read back CanWakeup=true. GET /api/wol/device/wakeup returned ret=0; an AF_PACKET capture bound only to the TEST bridge observed one exact 102-byte standard magic packet destined for UDP/9. The configured random device Port was not used. The device was deleted, the original disabled service configuration restored, the empty device baseline rechecked, and the disposable container/network removed. No shutdown call was made.

observations.packet: The captured UDP payload exactly matched ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff plus the six-byte TEST MAC repeated sixteen times, for a total payload size of 102 bytes
observations.port: Observed wake destination was UDP/9; the separately configured random device Port differed and was not used for the emitted wake datagram
observations.device_state: Before wake, the TEST device reported CanWakeup=true and State=Unknown. No claim is made that a real host became online because the target was an isolated synthetic device
observations.schema: The TEST device readback contained BroadcastIPs as an array whose populated item was a string broadcast address
observations.cleanup: The owned TEST device was deleted, Server/Client returned to the original disabled baseline, no WOL devices remained, and the disposable internal network/container were removed

wol_ci_behavior.security: The probe refuses to run outside GitHub Actions. It does not address a physical NIC, LAN broadcast domain or real MAC; the only wake target is a private Docker --internal bridge broadcast address.
